title: Implement Min Heap
statement:
You need to implement the Min Heap with the following given methods.

- insert (x) -> insert value x to the min heap
- getMin -> Output the minimum value from min heap
- exctractMin -> Remove the minimum element from the heap
- heapSize -> return the current size of the heap
- isEmpty -> returns if heap is empty or not
- changeKey (ind, val) -> update the value at given index to val (index will be given 0-based indexing)
- initializeHeap -> Initialize the heap

**Example 1:**

```
$7a
```

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.body: The heap is usually stored in an array. An empty list can represent an initial empty heap.

hints.title: Hint 2
hints.body: Add x to the end of the array. The smallest element is always at index 0. Swap the root (minimum element) with the last element. Return the length of the array representing the heap. Return True if the array is empty, otherwise False.

doubts.question: Why do we heapify-up on insertion but heapify-down on deletion?
doubts.answer:
Insertion: New elements start at the bottom, so we move up to fix order.
Deletion: The last element is moved to the top, so we move down to fix order.

followUps.question: How would this be implemented for a dynamic streaming dataset (priority queue)?
followUps.answer: Use a self-balancing heap to maintain real-time priority ordering.

followUps.question: How does this extend to a d-ary heap (e.g., ternary heap with 3 children per node)?
followUps.answer:
Instead of 2*i+1 and 2*i+2, use d*i+1, d*i+2, ..., d*i+d for children.
Heapify operations check among d children instead of 2.

facts: Min-heaps power priority queues in operating systems, event simulators, and job schedulers, always exposing the next smallest-priority item for processing.
Graph algorithms such as Dijkstra’s shortest-path method use min-heaps to repeatedly select the currently closest unexplored vertex.
